justification: I independently re-verified every load-bearing claim rather than trust the article's own account of it, and found zero factual errors. (1) Core algorithm and trace: I reimplemented the lazy-deletion Dijkstra from scratch with my own graph and names (S/X/Y/Z/W/T instead of A/B/C/D/E/F, weights renamed but same topology) and got the identical shape of result the article shows -- 9 pops for 6 vertices, 3 stale duplicates caught by the visited-set check, correct final distances. (2) Negative-edge counterexample: I built a *different* 3-node graph (P->Q weight 2, P->R weight 6, R->Q weight -8, vs. the article's 1/4/-5) and ran my own Dijkstra, my own brute-force enumerator, and my own from-scratch Bellman-Ford. Dijkstra returned 2; brute force and Bellman-Ford both independently returned -2 (via P->R->Q). This confirms, on a graph the writer never saw, that Dijkstra really does return a wrong answer under a negative edge and that the mechanism the article describes (the vertex finalizes on its direct edge before the cheaper edge through the negative-weight neighbor is even examined) is the correct explanation, not just a property of the article's specific numbers. (3) A* vs. plain Dijkstra: I built a different 9x10 maze and confirmed both searches agree on the optimal path length (17) while A* expands strictly fewer nodes (52 vs. 58) -- same qualitative result the article reports on its own maze (17 steps, 34 vs. 53 expanded), reproduced independently rather than copied. (4) PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority> claims: I fetched the MS Learn class page, the Remove method page, the Dequeue method page, and the dotnet/runtime PriorityQueue.cs source directly. Every quoted fragment is verbatim and correctly attached: 'Implements an array-backed, quaternary min-heap' and 'does not guarantee first-in-first-out semantics for elements of equal priority' (class Remarks), 'The method performs a linear-time scan of every element in the heap, removing the first value found to match the element parameter' (Remove Remarks), and the empty-queue InvalidOperationException on Dequeue (Exceptions section). The runtime source confirms the backing field is literally `private (TElement Element, TPriority Priority)[] _nodes;` with no auxiliary index, and Remove's FindIndex is a plain O(n) loop over _nodes -- exactly what the article claims, and I did not just take the article's word for the source reading. (5) Sedgewick & Wayne quotes: I fetched algs4.cs.princeton.edu/44sp/ and /24pq/ directly and confirmed all five quoted fragments (the relax-and-add description, the LazyDijkstraSP exercise text, the Bellman-Ford EV-time description, the DijkstraSP negative-weight exception text, and the O(E log V) Dijkstra proposition, plus the 1+lg n / 2 lg n heap-compare proposition) are verbatim on those pages and support exactly the sentences they're attached to -- no misattribution, no claim the source doesn't make. (6) DOI-only citations: Dijkstra 1959 is cited once, for the uncontroversial, well-known fact that Dijkstra published the algorithm in that 1959 paper; Hart/Nilsson/Raphael 1968 is cited once, for the equally uncontroversial fact that they introduced A* as a generalization of best-first search in that paper. Neither citation carries a verbatim quote, a page-specific claim, or any assertion that isn't common knowledge in the field -- the restraint the writer described is genuinely followed. (7) Determinism / tie-order risk: I ran run-code.mjs 5 times total and got byte-identical PASS results every time, including on the exact D/F priority-6 tie the article calls out (F final, then D stale, every run). This is expected and not really 'flaky' in the CI sense: .NET's PriorityQueue has no randomization, so a fixed insertion order on a fixed runtime build always resolves a tie the same way -- the risk the class docs (and the article) correctly flag is only across a *different* .NET version, which would fail run-code.mjs deterministically and loudly on that build, not intermittently. The one gap is that the `text output` blocks pin the exact D/F pop order with no `[...]` wildcard, so a future .NET SDK bump that changes quaternary-heap tie resolution would surface as an unexplained run-code failure on this one line rather than something self-evidently a tie-order artifact -- a minor, easily-fixed robustness gap, not a correctness problem today. Compared against the top current results for 'Dijkstra's algorithm C#' (GeeksforGeeks's version, which I fetched: five-language code dump, no decrease-key/PriorityQueue-limits discussion, no formal correctness argument, and a negative-edge paragraph with no worked counterexample) and Wikipedia's algorithm page (pseudocode and a general description, no language-specific priority-queue analysis at all), this article is substantially deeper: a real cut-argument correctness proof, a genuinely verified negative-edge failure, an honest decrease-key-vs-relinquish-and-reinsert cost tradeoff with its own exercise, and an A* section that measures node expansion rather than asserting it helps. That clears the 8.5 MDN-quality bar comfortably; the two nits below are the only things keeping it short of a 10.

issues.location: "Why picking the cheapest frontier vertex is safe" section, the sentence "If P uses only already-finalized vertices, it cannot be shorter than d, because those vertices' distances are already known correct and d already accounts for the best edge out of them."
issues.problem: This case of the cut argument is correct but relies on an inductive fact -- that every finalized vertex's outgoing edges have already been relaxed by the time u is considered -- that the sentence gestures at ('already accounts for') without stating. A strong student could read 'd already accounts for the best edge out of them' and not see why that's guaranteed rather than assumed, since it's the one place the proof leans on the algorithm's own bookkeeping instead of pure logic.
issues.fixLooksLike: Add one clause making the induction explicit, e.g.: "...because relaxation happens the moment a vertex is finalized, so every finalized vertex's edge into u was already considered before u's current tentative distance d was set."
